title: Dinah and the Massacre at Shechem
summary: While Jacob's family is living near Shechem, the son of the city's ruler seizes Jacob's daughter Dinah and lies with her by force, then asks to marry her. Jacob's sons answer deceitfully, agreeing to intermarriage if every man of the city is circumcised. While the men are still in pain, Simeon and Levi kill them all, and their brothers plunder the city, leaving Jacob afraid for his family's survival.
story: Jacob has just arrived safely at Shechem, bought land, and built an altar to the God of Israel (33:18-20). This chapter shows what happens when that family settles down beside a Canaanite city. It is one of the darkest chapters in Genesis, and God is never mentioned in it. Dinah, the daughter born to Leah (30:21), is violated; her brothers answer with deceit and slaughter; and Jacob, silent through most of it, speaks only to complain of the danger to himself. The chapter explains why Simeon and Levi lose their standing when Jacob blesses his sons at the end of his life (49:5-7), and it presses a question Genesis keeps asking: would Abraham's family keep its distinct calling, or be absorbed into the peoples around it? In chapter 35 God will call Jacob away from Shechem and back to Bethel.
historical:
Canaan in this period was a patchwork of small city-states, each ruled from a walled town by its own leader, and Shechem was one of the most important in the hill country. Hamor is called a Hivite, one of the peoples Genesis lists among the inhabitants of Canaan (10:17); the Gibeonites who later tricked Joshua into a treaty were also Hivites (Joshua 9:7). Shechem is the prince of the region, the son of its ruling family, and the city and the man share a name. The family's name lasted: centuries later, in the days of the judges, a rebel in Shechem urged the city to serve “the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem” (Judges 9:28).

The negotiations take place at the city gate (verse 20), where elders and citizens met to settle public business, and the men of the city agree together. For Jacob's family, herdsmen with no city of their own, the danger afterward was real. As Jacob says, they were few among the Canaanites and Perizzites, and an alliance of towns could have destroyed them. In the next chapter a terror from God falls on the surrounding cities so that no one pursues them (35:5).
cultural:
The chapter assumes a world where marriages were arranged between families and a woman's honor was bound up with theirs. Shechem's act was a crime against Dinah and, in her brothers' eyes, an assault on the whole household. His father then negotiates as if this were an ordinary marriage proposal, offering a bride-price and gifts of any size (verse 12). A marriage payment was normal, and Israel's later law required a man who seized an unbetrothed young woman to pay her father and marry her, with no right ever to divorce her (Deuteronomy 22:28-29), a provision meant to secure her future in a society where she might otherwise never marry. But Shechem is holding Dinah in his house while he bargains (verse 26), and her brothers hear his offer as an insult.

Circumcision was practiced by some peoples of the region, the Egyptians among them, but not by these Canaanites, and for Abraham's family it was the sign of the covenant God made with Abraham (Genesis 17). Jacob's sons turn that sign into bait, knowing that grown men would be at their weakest a few days after the cutting, when pain and swelling were worst. Hamor and Shechem, for their part, sell the deal to their city by promising that Jacob's livestock and property will become theirs (verse 23). Neither side is dealing honestly.
literary: The chapter is built around who speaks and who doesn't. Dinah never says a word, and we never learn what she felt or what became of her. Jacob stays silent until the very end. Shechem, Hamor, and the brothers do the talking, and the talk is bargaining. The narrator's judgments come through word choice. Shechem “defiled” Dinah (verses 5, 13, 27), a word for making unclean, and his act was “an outrage in Israel” (verse 7), a phrase later used of sexual crimes that tore at the community's covenant life, as when Tamar pleaded with Amnon that “such a thing should never be done in Israel” (2 Samuel 13:12). The brothers answer “deceitfully” (verse 13), with the same word Isaac used of Jacob's theft of the blessing (27:35); the deceiver's sons have learned his trade. The chapter ends not with a verdict but with two speeches that talk past each other. Jacob worries about his reputation and safety, and his sons ask, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” The question is left hanging, and Jacob's real answer comes only on his deathbed (49:5-7).

outline.t: Shechem seizes Dinah and demands her as his wife
The men of Shechem are circumcised
Simeon and Levi's massacre and the plunder of the city
Jacob's rebuke and his sons' reply

doctrines.note: Sin compounds. A man's violent desire leads to a bargain, the bargain to deceit, deceit to massacre, and massacre to the plunder of women and children who had done nothing. Every party is guilty of something, and the chapter lets none of them become a hero.

Genesis doesn't approve the brothers' revenge. Jacob's last words curse their anger and cruelty (49:5-7), and Israel's law later forbade putting anyone to death for another's sin (Deuteronomy 24:16). Wrong demands justice, but vengeance that falls on a whole town is a new wrong, not justice.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, and here it is emptied twice: offered to Shechem's men as a business term with no faith attached, and used by Jacob's sons as a trap. A covenant sign cut loose from the covenant God can become a weapon.

words.note: Anah, to humble, afflict, or violate. It is used of sexual assault here and in the stories of Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12, 14) and the Levite's concubine (Judges 19:24), naming an act that degrades and wrongs a woman. Most interpreters read verse 2 as rape, as the BSB does; a few scholars argue that the verb stresses the dishonor of sex outside proper marriage rather than force. Either way, the text counts it a grave wrong done to Dinah.

Mirmah, deceit. The brothers answer Shechem and Hamor with it (verse 13). It is the word Isaac used when he told Esau, “Your brother came deceitfully” (27:35). Jacob's trickery has reproduced itself in his sons, and it will surface again when they deceive their father about Joseph (37:31-33).

Nevalah, outrage or disgraceful folly. It doesn't mean mere silliness; it names an act that breaks the moral bonds holding a community together. It is used of grave sexual wrongs elsewhere (Deuteronomy 22:21; Judges 19:23; 2 Samuel 13:12), and here the narrator judges Shechem's act by the standards of the people Jacob's family would become.

christ: There is no prediction of Christ in this chapter, and it would be wrong to force one. What the chapter does is show, without softening, the family through which the promised blessing would come: Levi, whose descendants became Israel's priests, and the brothers of Judah, from whom Jesus was born. The Bible never pretends the Messiah's ancestors were clean. The chapter also sets two failed answers to evil side by side, the brothers' vengeance and Jacob's self-concern. The gospel offers another. Paul told the Christians in Rome, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19), and Jesus did not take vengeance but bore violence himself at the cross, while the New Testament insists that God will judge every wrong. Finally, the misuse of circumcision here anticipates a theme the prophets and apostles developed: the outward sign means nothing without a changed heart, for “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit” (Romans 2:29).

hard.q: Were Simeon and Levi right to avenge their sister, and why is this story in the Bible?
hard.a:
The brothers' anger has real grounds. Their sister was violated and was being held in her attacker's house while he negotiated for her, and their father did nothing. Their closing question is not a foolish one. Some later readers admired their zeal; the book of Judith, a Jewish work from about the second or first century BC that Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive as Scripture and Protestants place in the Apocrypha, praises Simeon's act.

Genesis doesn't share that admiration. The brothers use a sacred sign as a trap and kill every man of a city for the crime of one, and their brothers carry off women and children as plunder, making still more victims. Jacob's objection in verse 30 is self-centered, but his final word is not: on his deathbed he says of Simeon and Levi, “Cursed be their anger, for it is strong, and their wrath, for it is cruel!” (49:7). The story is in the Bible because Scripture tells the truth about the people God chose, including the violence done to a woman and the violence done in her name. It makes heroes of no one, and its silence about Dinah's own voice is part of its indictment. Readers who carry this kind of harm themselves may find the chapter painful; they deserve to be heard and helped, by people they trust and by those trained to care for them.

questions: Dinah never speaks in this chapter. Whose voices go unheard when a family or community responds to harm, and how could they be heard?
Jacob said nothing, and his sons did far too much. What does a faithful response to serious wrongdoing look like between silence and revenge?
The brothers used a sacred sign as a weapon. In what ways can religious language or practice be turned into a tool for other ends?
